lessonRef.title: Concept model A: asking and answering text-dependent questions

studentTask.text: This Grade 5 lesson develops asking and answering text-dependent questions within the unit “Reading and Writing Community.” Read the delivered Academy-original source before responding. Strong ELA work separates what the source explicitly says from what a reader infers, selects evidence because it is relevant and sufficient, and explains the connection instead of leaving a quotation to speak for itself. Today's concept model a work asks you to make that reasoning visible and to revise if the evidence does not support the first idea.

sourceReference.text:
[1] Near the end of the “Reading and Writing Community” workshop at the neighborhood library, Priya reviewed two witness notes about the same event. The first portfolio note claimed, “My final piece is better because I worked harder.” The claim may have been sincere, but it gave a reader no visible way to inspect the growth.

[2] Xavier suggested comparing one paragraph from each version. The early paragraph listed three facts without showing their relationship. The later paragraph grouped two facts as evidence, explained the connection, and set aside the third because it did not support the controlling idea. The change was specific enough to discuss.

[3] A second comparison revealed a tradeoff. The later opening was clearer, but it had lost an image that gave the earlier draft energy. Rather than calling every revision an improvement, Priya restored the image in a new position and recorded why clarity and voice both mattered for the intended audience.

[4] The reflection used asking and answering text-dependent questions to turn a vague statement of pride into an evidence-based account. It named a change, located proof in the work, and explained the decision behind it. It also named a next step, because publication marked the best current version rather than the end of learning.

[5] Before revising, the group tested the source against the workshop goal: asking and answering text-dependent questions. They highlighted language that supported the goal, circled a detail that complicated it, and drew an arrow where the relationship between two ideas needed to be made explicit. The marks produced different possible readings, so the group had to defend priorities rather than copy a single approved answer.

guidedSupport.text:
Use this source-specific routine for “Reading Lab 2: asking and answering text-dependent questions”:
1. Preview the title and paragraph structure; write what asking and answering text-dependent questions asks you to notice or do.
2. Mark one statement the source makes explicitly and one inference a reader could draw. Keep the two kinds of thinking separate.
3. Test the inference with the evidence requirement in today's task. If the evidence is weak or incomplete, narrow or revise the inference.
4. Draft your own response. A facilitator may clarify directions or ask questions, but may not supply your claim, evidence choice, sentences, or revision.

independentEvidenceTask.text:
Read “Reading Lab 2: asking and answering text-dependent questions,” then answer: Trace how one example in the reading demonstrates asking and answering text-dependent questions. Which step in the example does the most work?

Deliverable: Grade 5: a labeled explanation of the example and its most important step; write one developed paragraph.

Evidence requirement: Use two quoted or paraphrased details with paragraph numbers. Label source evidence with a paragraph number or another precise location. Your response must explain the connection between the evidence and your conclusion.

remediation.text:
If asking and answering text-dependent questions is not yet secure, return to “Reading Lab 2: asking and answering text-dependent questions” before starting over:
- Evidence gap: underline the exact words that support the idea and label their paragraph or location.
- Reasoning gap: complete the stem “This evidence matters because …” in your own words, then reread the question.
- Overclaim: name what the source does not establish and narrow the conclusion to what the evidence can support.
- Completion gap: compare the draft with each learner success criterion and repair one missing part at a time.

extension.text: Apply asking and answering text-dependent questions to a different paragraph or a defensible alternative interpretation of “Reading Lab 2: asking and answering text-dependent questions.” Compare the new result with your first response and explain which evidence changes, which reasoning still holds, and why.
